for a while.example: and the snow helped, for a while

for ages.example: You've had those candles for ages and you never knew what they could do.
for ages.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

for good.example: or if they've all gone for good."
for good.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

get lost.example: "Get lost, spy!" hissed Asa, pushing Tancred backward.
get lost.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

get the better of.meaning: (Of a feeling) To become too strong for you to control.

get the better of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

give it a go.example: "But, hey, I'll give it a go."

gloom and doom.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

go on.meaning: (1) To continue speaking or doing something; to keep happening ("The Hundred Heads' dinner went on and on and on"). (2) Said to tell someone to start or to continue.

going on.example: You must've heard what's been going on.
going on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

grit his teeth.meaning: To press your teeth together; to be brave or patient when something is hard.

his heart sank.meaning: He suddenly felt sad or worried.

hold on.meaning: Wait a moment; or hold something tightly.

hold sway.meaning: To have power or control (in a place).

hold sway.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in a daze.meaning: Not able to think clearly, because of a shock.

in for it.meaning: Going to be punished or get into trouble.

in for it.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in single file.meaning: In one line, one person behind another.

in single file.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in spite of.meaning: Although something is true; not stopped by.

in the end.example: In the end he told himself he had to go.

in the meantime.meaning: During the time before something happens.

in the meantime.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in time.meaning: (1) (Just in time) Not late; before it is too late. (2) After some time; in the end ("We'll find out in time").

in time.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in unison.meaning: All together, at the same time.
in unison.example: asked Gabriel and Charlie in unison.
in unison.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

keep an eye on.meaning: To watch someone or something carefully, to keep them safe.

keep an eye on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

let out.meaning: (1) To let someone go out of a place; to set someone free ("someone let him out"). (2) To make a sound or give out a smell (a yell, a cry, a sigh).

let out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

look forward to.meaning: To feel happy about something that is going to happen.

look forward to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

make for.meaning: (1) To move toward a place. (2) "Made for" someone = made to be used by that person ("made for the baby who was born nine days before Queen Berenice died").

make for.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

make out.meaning: To see or hear something with difficulty.

make out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

make sure.meaning: To check or do something so that you are certain.
make sure.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

make the best of.meaning: To do as well as you can in a bad situation.
make the best of.example: As usual, she made the best of things.
make the best of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

no doubt.example: "A key, no doubt," said Uncle Paton with a small yawn.
no doubt.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

nothing to do with.meaning: (Have nothing to do with) Not connected with; not wanting any contact with.
nothing to do with.example: They wanted nothing to do with me.
nothing to do with.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

now now.meaning: Kind words you say to calm someone down. It does not mean "at this time".
now now.example: "Now, now, now. Let's all calm down," said Mrs. Onimous

of all people.meaning: Said to show surprise that this person did it.
of all people.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

off guard.meaning: (Caught/thrown off guard) Surprised, not ready for something.
off guard.example: Caught off guard, Charlie mumbled, "Oh, no one, really.
off guard.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

oh dear.meaning: What you say when you are worried, sad or a little upset. It is not about a dear person.

oh well.meaning: What you say when something is not good, but you accept it and go on.

on either side.example: To Charlie, the children sitting on either side of Manfred seemed especially smug tonight.
on either side.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

on the other hand.meaning: Used to give the opposite fact or idea.
on the other hand.example: His uncle, on the other hand, had a very bad time.
on the other hand.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

on the verge of.example: She was in my house, on the verge of selling it.
on the verge of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

out of breath.meaning: Breathing fast and hard, after running.
out of breath.example: Charlie felt quite out of breath when Billy finally came to a halt.
out of breath.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

out of reach.meaning: Too far away to touch or catch.
out of reach.example: he waited just out of reach of the last pair of legs.
out of reach.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

out of their wits.meaning: (Scare someone out of their wits) To frighten someone very much.
out of their wits.example: it's so much fun scaring people out of their wits.
out of their wits.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

pick up.meaning: (1) To lift something from a surface. (2) To come and collect someone ("Your uncle will pick you up"). (3) A "pick-me-up" is food or drink that makes you feel better.
pick up.example: Billy picked up the rat and began talking in his strange, piping rat-speak.
pick up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

point of view.meaning: A way of thinking about something; how one person sees it.
point of view.example: "Histories are written from a certain point of view," Bartholomew said dismissively.
point of view.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

put his foot down.meaning: To press the car pedal hard and drive faster.
put his foot down.example: Paton put his foot down and they bumped over the cobblestones and out of the square.
put his foot down.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

put two and two together.meaning: To guess the truth from the facts you know.
put two and two together.example: "Should I put two and two together and guess why you've come?"
put two and two together.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

put up with.meaning: To accept something unpleasant without complaining.
put up with.example: Though, with little Una around, he was having to put up with a rather rough grooming.
put up with.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

run away.meaning: To leave a place quickly and secretly, to escape.
run away.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

safe as houses.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

see the error of her ways.meaning: To understand that you have done wrong.
see the error of her ways.example: was that she could never see the error of her ways.
see the error of her ways.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

set off.example: As soon as his coat was on, he and his uncle set off.
set off.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

set to work.example: While Tancred set to work, the cats sped down the hillside into the city.
set to work.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

shut up.example: "Shut up and go to sleep," said Fidelio.
shut up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

sit up.meaning: To move from lying down to sitting.
sit up.example: Billy Raven groaned and sat up.
sit up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

slip away.meaning: To leave quietly, so that nobody notices.

slip away.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

spin on his heel.example: Benjamin spun on his heel, staring around the square.
spin on his heel.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

stand his ground.meaning: To stay where you are and not run away or give in.

stand his ground.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

suit yourself.meaning: Do what you want (said when you do not care, or are a little annoyed).
suit yourself.example: "Suit yourself." Paton ambled back into the kitchen.
suit yourself.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

swimming against the tide.meaning: Trying to do something that most people or things are against; a fight you cannot win.
swimming against the tide.example: "There's no future in swimming against the tide.
swimming against the tide.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

take a deep breath.meaning: To breathe in a lot of air, often before saying something hard.
take a deep breath.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

take care.meaning: (1) Be careful (said when you say goodbye). (2) "Take care of" = look after ("he couldn't take care of himself").
take care.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

take off.example: Billy took off his glasses, which had steamed up.
take off.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

tamper with.meaning: To change or damage something secretly, so that it does harm.
tamper with.example: Someone tampered with them, and it must have been one of them
tamper with.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

the worse for wear.meaning: Damaged, dirty or tired after a hard time.

the worse for wear.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

trouble brewing.meaning: (There is trouble brewing) Something bad is starting to happen.

turn into.meaning: To change and become something different.

what on earth.meaning: Said to show great surprise, like "what?".

fast asleep.example: He saw Charlie, fast asleep in bed.

paragraphs.context: Naren can send shadow words over great distances.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Naren Bloor can send messages with shadows.
paragraphs.simple: This is from the list of characters at the start of the book. Naren is the adopted daughter of Bartholomew Bloor. She can send words as shadows to people far away.

background.note: A magician-king who came out of Africa long ago. All the endowed children are descended from his ten children.
A Welsh magician from long ago, the Red King's good friend.
The old, gray boarding school where Charlie studies music, art or drama. Endowed children must go there.
A girl from China, Bartholomew Bloor's adopted daughter. She is endowed: she can send 'shadow words'.
The Red King's eldest son, a cruel tyrant. Manfred is descended from him.

paragraphs.context: Olivia is an illusionist.
paragraphs.simple: This is from the list of endowed children at the start of the book. Olivia can make people see things that are not really there. The Bloors do not know about her gift.

background.note: A lively drama student at Bloor's who loves wild clothes and colored hair. She becomes one of Charlie's best friends.
A daughter of the Red King who fled his castle and married an Italian prince. She tried to cure the deadly boa.

paragraphs.context: The Red King and his friend walked together through the forest.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Red King walks into the forest with his friend.
paragraphs.simple: This prologue happens long ago. The Red King is still a man, but he is very sad. He walks with his friend Mathonwy, a magician.

paragraphs.context: Ten paces behind the men came three leopards;
paragraphs.mainIdea: The king's three old leopards follow him.
paragraphs.simple: The leopards are old now, but they always watch the king. They love him and would follow him anywhere.

background.note: The Red King's three faithful leopards, big wild cats that followed him into the forest.

paragraphs.context: It was said. Mathonwy shuddered. The king was leaving.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mathonwy learns that the king is leaving.
paragraphs.simple: The king has told the leopards to find a new master. Mathonwy is very sad, because the king has been his friend and teacher for a long time.

paragraphs.context: "Guard my children with your wild hearts.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The king gives the leopards a new job.
paragraphs.simple: The king says a spell. He asks the leopards to guard the families of his children and to stay wild in their hearts.

paragraphs.context: "Behold! Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The leopards have become three cats.
paragraphs.simple: The spell has changed the three leopards into cats with fire-colored coats: Aries, Leo and Sagittarius. These are the Flames, who help Charlie.

paragraphs.context: "Shape-shifting is not what I need, Mathonwy.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The king wants to change forever.
paragraphs.simple: The king could change his shape easily, but he wants a change that lasts forever. He is tired of his human life and wants a quieter form.

paragraphs.context: Last night I saw a boy in the clouds and I knew that he was one of mine.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The king sees a future child.
paragraphs.simple: The king tells Mathonwy about a boy he saw in the clouds. The boy will come from the king's family and from Mathonwy's family too.

paragraphs.context: beneath his arms slim green shoots sprouted from his body.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The king starts to turn into a tree.
paragraphs.simple: Mathonwy uses his wand, and green shoots grow from the king's body. The king grows taller and becomes a tree.

paragraphs.context: But the tears flowed on, coursing down the trunk, red as blood.
paragraphs.simple: Even as a tree, the king is still crying. His tears run down the trunk, and they are red like blood.

paragraphs.context: It stopped outside number twelve and three figures stumbled out.
paragraphs.simple: A car stops on Filbert Street in the snow. A man, a woman and a boy get out with their bags.

background.note: The street where Charlie lives, at number nine. Benjamin lives across the road at number twelve.

paragraphs.context: In the kitchen he warmed a pan of milk and poured it into three saucers.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie goes quietly downstairs with the three cats. He gives them warm milk and then some turkey.

paragraphs.context: Charlie looked anxiously at the door.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie is afraid Grandma Bone will hear.
paragraphs.simple: Billy sits very still and listens to the cats. Charlie is worried, because the cats are very loud and Grandma Bone might hear them.

background.note: Charlie's grandmother, his father's mother. She was born a Yewbeam. She is cold and bossy and spies on Charlie.
A small white-haired orphan who lives at Bloor's Academy. He is endowed: he can talk to animals.

paragraphs.context: the cats skimmed up the creeper and dropped down into a snowy field.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The cats run on through the snow.
paragraphs.simple: The cats run along the side of a big building to a high stone wall. They climb up the ivy and jump down into a snowy field.

paragraphs.context: A small shudder passed through the earth;
paragraphs.simple: Humans do not feel it, but the animals do. Birds scream, small animals run to hide, and dogs howl in the cold night.

paragraphs.context: It was a recently acquired habit and often made his friends laugh.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie has a funny new habit.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie runs back up the lane in the cold. He jumps in the air and claps his feet together, and this often makes his friends laugh.

paragraphs.context: He was an extraordinarily optimistic boy.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie always hopes for the best.
paragraphs.simple: Nothing makes Charlie sad for long. He is sure that his father is alive and that he will find him one day. His mother Amy has stopped hoping.

background.note: Charlie's kind, gentle mother. She works in a fruit and vegetable shop and misses Charlie's lost father.

paragraphs.context: Even Amy's mother, Maisie, could be heard gently snoring
paragraphs.simple: It is early on Saturday. Everyone at number nine is asleep except Amy, who tiptoes past Maisie's room.

background.note: Charlie's other grandmother, his mother's mother. She is warm, noisy and loving, and lives with Charlie's family.

paragraphs.context: "Charlie's just fine," said Amy.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Amy lets Benjamin into the house.
paragraphs.simple: Amy is going to work. She opens the door of number nine and lets Benjamin in, so he can surprise Charlie.

background.note: Charlie's best friend, who lives across Filbert Street. He is not endowed and goes to a different school.

paragraphs.context: He was a small fair-haired boy with a perpetually lost expression.
paragraphs.simple: Benjamin is happy that nothing has changed in Charlie's house. He is tired from his journey, but he wants to see Charlie and his dog Runner Bean.

background.note: Benjamin's big, friendly yellow dog. He often helps Charlie and his friends.

paragraphs.context: "Now, now, now. Let's all calm down," said Mrs. Onimous,
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. Onimous tries to calm everyone down. She pours boiling water into a huge teapot and tells the boys to eat some cake.

background.note: Onoria Onimous, Mr. Onimous's tall, gentle wife with a very long nose. She makes the cakes at the Pets' Café.

paragraphs.context: Billy took off his glasses, which had steamed up.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Billy tells what the animals saw.
paragraphs.simple: Billy repeats a story he heard from animals. Someone opened a door to a tunnel, and all the animals left through the castle ruin, down a cliff and over a bridge.

paragraphs.context: "Billy, there's nothing on the other side of the river," said Mr. Onimous.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr. Onimous talks about the river.
paragraphs.simple: Mr. Onimous says there is nothing across the river. It is a wild, empty place.

background.note: Orvil Onimous, a small furry-looking man who runs the Pets' Café and does pest control with the Flame cats.
A wild, empty area across the river from the city, where strange things happen.

paragraphs.context: They all piled into the small living room at the back of the store,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Emma tells her friends about the missing animals.
paragraphs.simple: The children go into the room behind the bookshop. Emma tells them that her duck Nancy is gone, and that there are no birds or animals left in the city.

background.note: A quiet art student with long blond hair. She is endowed: she can turn into a bird and fly.

paragraphs.context: He dropped gloomily onto his bed and thought of Benjamin,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie feels bad about Runner Bean.
paragraphs.simple: Runner Bean has disappeared. Benjamin waited seven months to see his dog, and Charlie feels it is his fault, because the dog was in his care.

paragraphs.context: At least ten children had lost their pets.
paragraphs.simple: At school, many children have lost their pets. Gabriel has lost twenty gerbils, three ducks and his mother's goat.

background.note: An endowed music student. He can feel other people's feelings and memories by wearing their clothes. He keeps gerbils.

paragraphs.context: "That's not as bad as losing your dog," whined Gwyneth Howells,
paragraphs.simple: Gwyneth has only a small problem, but she complains anyway. The writer calls her "a moaner", someone who often complains.

background.note: A girl in the music department at Bloor's Academy who plays the harp. Rosie Stubbs is her best friend.

paragraphs.context: Miss Chrystal, the violin teacher, gave Charlie a cheery wave from the door.
paragraphs.simple: The violin teacher waves at Charlie and asks if he is all right. She says he looks lost.

background.note: A cheerful music teacher at Bloor's who teaches strings, such as the violin.

paragraphs.context: "They came to see me, too," said Charlie, almost to himself.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie has an idea about the animals.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie thinks someone has found an object that links our world to an ancient spirit. The older boys listen with interest, but they are not sure they believe him.

paragraphs.context: Joshua was magnetic in more ways than one.
paragraphs.simple: Joshua Tilpin comes in covered with bits of paper and leaves, because things stick to him. Then come the twins Idith and Inez, and Billy, who has news for Charlie.

background.note: A strange new boy with paper stuck in his hair. He is endowed with magnetism: things and people are drawn to him.
Telekinetic twin girls at Bloor's Academy, relatives of Zelda Dobinski. They can move things with their minds.

paragraphs.context: Dorcas Loom had once been a round and rosy, perpetually smiling girl.
paragraphs.simple: Dorcas used to be a happy, smiling girl. Now she is heavy and unfriendly. She sits between the Branko twins, who only smile when someone is in trouble.

background.note: A plump, cheerful-looking endowed girl at Bloor's Academy.

paragraphs.context: the storm boy joined the group making its way to the dormitories.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The children go up to bed.
paragraphs.simple: Tancred, the "storm boy", goes with the others to the dormitories. The older boys go up to the top floors, and Emma goes to the girls' rooms.

paragraphs.context: "Oh, poor Blessed, I forgot him."
paragraphs.simple: Billy runs to the bathroom and almost falls over Blessed, the short, fat old dog.

background.note: Cook's very old, ugly, wrinkled dog at Bloor's Academy. He talks to Billy Raven.

paragraphs.context: "For a dog, he described it very well," Billy said appreciatively.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Billy tells what a dog saw.
paragraphs.simple: Billy repeats what a dog told him. A woman came down the stairs with two shadows, and at the doors one shadow stood up and turned green with golden patterns.

paragraphs.context: said the first boy, a large, chunky character who had earned the name "Bragger" Braine.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A boy complains about the dog.
paragraphs.simple: A big boy says the dog smells. Everyone calls him "Bragger" Braine. A bragger is someone who boasts a lot.

background.note: A big, chunky bully at Bloor's Academy, often with Damian Smerk.

paragraphs.context: A greenish-gray alligator of gigantic proportions blocked the entire hall.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A huge alligator fills the hall.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie stares at the creature in front of him: a giant alligator with yellow eyes and a huge mouth full of sharp teeth.

paragraphs.context: The passage echoed with the drumbeats of hastily slammed doors.
paragraphs.simple: Behind the monster, some girls have fainted on the floor. Others look out of their rooms, scream and slam their doors.

paragraphs.context: Charlie recognized the voice of his great-aunt Lucretia, the matron.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie hears his great-aunt Lucretia, the matron. She does not like him, but suddenly the monster starts to disappear, from its tail to its head.

background.note: The eldest of Charlie's three great-aunts, Grandma Bone's sister. She is a strict, unkind woman.

paragraphs.context: He hated this part of the academy.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie feels that he does not belong in this part of the school. He wants to prove he did nothing wrong, but he must not say who really did it.

paragraphs.context: The huge flagstones were cracked and broken.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie runs into the courtyard and sees a mess. The big stones of the floor are cracked, and there is a dark hole where one large stone was.

paragraphs.context: It was the girl in sunshine yellow.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie sees the girl in yellow again.
paragraphs.simple: Early in the morning, Charlie sees a girl in a bright yellow coat under the frosty chestnut tree. A scarf covers her mouth, and she waves at him.

paragraphs.context: "The river," he gasped. "I didn't know it was so close."
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie looks down at the river.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie holds the railing of a bridge. Far below him, the river rushes over dark rocks, and the noise frightens him.

paragraphs.context: He'd told his mother that he wouldn't make any more hasty decisions,
paragraphs.simple: On his birthday, Charlie promised his mother to think before doing dangerous things. Now he is walking over an unsafe bridge above a deep river.

paragraphs.context: Animals of every description filled the enclosure.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie finds a place full of animals.
paragraphs.simple: At the end there is a small cottage with barns. Birds sit on the roof, and ponies, dogs and cats fill the field around it.

paragraphs.context: Charlie stayed where he was.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie does not want to leave the animals. He sees Emma's duck, Homer the owl, and two white rabbits that look like Olivia's.

paragraphs.context: He became aware that pictures covered every spare surface of the walls.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The room is full of mountain pictures.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie wants to speak to the woman, but he notices the pictures on the walls. They show many different views of a mountain.

paragraphs.context: In one of the pictures an explorer waved at the camera.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie hears the voice of a laughing explorer in a photo. Then the kitchen swings and disappears, and Charlie is alone in the picture.

paragraphs.context: Bartholomew Bloor married Mary Chance on a rainy, autumn morning.
paragraphs.simple: Bartholomew Bloor married Mary Chance, a poor dancer. Ezekiel and the Yewbeams hated her, and her parents were afraid for her.

background.note: Dr. Bloor's very old, evil grandfather. He lives in the west wing of the academy and uses dark magic.
Ezekiel's son, who has lived far away for many years. He returns with his adopted daughter Naren.
A young dancer who married Bartholomew Bloor long ago.

paragraphs.context: "One day a letter came from one of my exploring friends.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The speaker talks about his son Harold.
paragraphs.simple: The speaker loves to explore. His son Harold was eight and very different: Harold hated travel, camping and even picnics.

paragraphs.context: A thing they called The Shadow.
paragraphs.mainIdea: He is afraid of The Shadow.
paragraphs.simple: The speaker feels safe here from two terrible families, and from something he heard about in Italy, called The Shadow. He still dreams about it.

paragraphs.context: "You will find your father, Charlie," Bartholomew said with conviction.
paragraphs.simple: Bartholomew is sure that Charlie will find his father. He says Lyell is a good man, and that they became best friends long ago.

background.note: Lyell Bone, Charlie's father. Charlie was told that he died, but Charlie is sure he is still alive and wants to find him.

paragraphs.context: "Stop that thing jabbering," snarled Albert.
paragraphs.simple: Albert Loom is angry. He says that if no one tells them where their dogs are, they will take all the other animals.

background.note: Albert and Alfred Loom, Dorcas Loom's big, unpleasant older brothers. They keep four rottweiler dogs.

paragraphs.context: He rushed at the Looms, barking furiously.
paragraphs.simple: Runner Bean runs at the Loom brothers. But Albert and Alfred know how to handle big dogs. They pull him to the side and chain him to a lamppost.

paragraphs.context: A deep sound rumbled down the narrow alley:
paragraphs.simple: Three angry growls fill the alley. Joshua and the Looms step back, and then three flame-colored streaks fly at them and land on their shoulders.

paragraphs.context: "I don't know anything about the others.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie gets angry with Mrs. Brown.
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. Brown looks at Charlie as if he did something wrong. Charlie says he only found Runner Bean and brought him back, and he turns to leave.

background.note: Benjamin's parents. They are private detectives and are almost always busy with their work.

paragraphs.context: Before Charlie could answer, Rembrandt and Runner Bean were at it again.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The rat and the dog make a mess.
paragraphs.simple: Rembrandt the rat jumps onto a shelf, and Runner Bean tries to reach him. Books and toys fall down, and an angry Mrs. Brown opens the door.

background.note: A black rat. First Mr. Boldova's pet, later Billy Raven's. He can talk to Billy.

paragraphs.context: A smart-looking van pulled away from the opposite curb as the boys emerged,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie has something urgent to do.
paragraphs.simple: A van drives away as the boys come out, but Charlie does not think about it. He tells his friends he cannot play in the park because he has something important to do.

paragraphs.context: The Flames' warning rang in his ears: Watch your mother.
paragraphs.simple: The Flame cats told Charlie to watch his mother. He thought she was safe at home, and he wonders how he can watch her everywhere.

background.note: Three magic copper-colored cats, Aries, Leo and Sagittarius, who protect Charlie and the good endowed children.

paragraphs.context: he sensed that the Flames were already near.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie feels that the Flame cats are near. He sees them on a roof, and they climb down a tree and stand at his feet.

paragraphs.context: Grandma Bone stepped back, bleating, "Take them away."
paragraphs.mainIdea: Grandma Bone is afraid of the Flames.
paragraphs.simple: The three Flame cats walk up to the living room door and look in with glittering eyes. Grandma Bone steps back and wants them taken away.

paragraphs.context: Amy replaced the receiver. "His name's Doctor Tanaka."
paragraphs.simple: Amy has called a doctor on the phone. His name is Doctor Tanaka.

background.note: A young, kind doctor who comes to help when Maisie is frozen by a spell.

paragraphs.context: "And two endowments are better than one."
paragraphs.simple: The doctor says that every magic power can be broken. Two endowed people working together are stronger than one.

paragraphs.context: "It only took one prawn," Uncle Paton declared.
paragraphs.simple: Uncle Paton says one bad prawn was enough, and Maisie ate it. He thinks Venetia is to blame.

background.note: Charlie's great-uncle, Grandma Bone's brother. He hides from daylight because his endowment makes lights burst. He helps Charlie.
The youngest great-aunt, Grandma Bone's sister. She is vain and makes dangerous enchanted clothes.

paragraphs.context: Don't close your curtains tonight.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie thinks about a strange message.
paragraphs.simple: Someone told Charlie not to close his curtains tonight. He wonders what her gift could be. A white moth lands on the curtain as he opens it.

paragraphs.context: as the shadows climbed the bedpost and crawled across the covers.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie sees small shadows climb up his bed. They run over his hands and up his sleeve, but he cannot feel them.

paragraphs.context: And I stole some vervain from Great-aunt Eustacia's garden,
paragraphs.simple: Charlie reminds his mother how they once helped Uncle Paton. He took a plant called vervain from Great-aunt Eustacia's garden, and they made tea with it.

background.note: The middle great-aunt, Grandma Bone's sister. She has an iron-gray bun and sometimes sees the future.
A wild plant (herb). People once believed it could cure illness and protect them from magic.

paragraphs.context: Mrs. Gunn had become her closest, perhaps her only, friend,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Amy visits her friend Mrs. Gunn.
paragraphs.simple: Amy is helping Mrs. Gunn clean her messy kitchen. Amy likes it there, and Mrs. Gunn is her best friend.

paragraphs.context: Green marble pillars stood on either side of the entrance,
paragraphs.simple: On her way home, Amy looks at a splendid building on High Street. Its many windows shine with soft light, as if it is full of treasures.

paragraphs.context: velvet-covered counters displayed exquisite jewelry, silk scarves,
paragraphs.mainIdea: The store is full of expensive things.
paragraphs.simple: Inside, Amy sees jewelry, silk scarves and perfumes. The prices are so high that she does not dare to think about them.

paragraphs.context: Amy got out on the top floor.
paragraphs.simple: On the top floor, the floor is covered with thick black fur. A very handsome man comes out of a door, and Amy suddenly worries about her old coat and shoes.

paragraphs.context: The man took her hand and bent over it like a hungry animal.
paragraphs.simple: The handsome man tells Amy his name, Hart Noble. He bends over her hand like a hungry animal and says the carpet is made of arctic bear.

background.note: A charming, rich man whom Amy Bone meets at Kingdom's store.

paragraphs.context: It didn't bother Charlie that half the boys in his dormitory wouldn't speak to him.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie opens his curtains at night.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie waits until the other boys are asleep. Then he opens the curtains a little and lets a thin line of moonlight into the room.

paragraphs.context: The sky was crowded with birds.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Huge flocks of birds fill the sky.
paragraphs.simple: While Charlie sleeps, thousands of birds fly over the city. They land on walls and trees and go to sleep. Only the owls stay awake.

paragraphs.context: It's the Hundred Heads' dinner on Friday and the Grand Ball on Saturday.
paragraphs.simple: There is a big dinner on Friday and a ball on Saturday. Dr. Bloor wants no children in the building, but Matron will not cancel Charlie's detention.

background.note: The head of Bloor's Academy. A big, stern man with small black eyes. He is Manfred's father.
A meeting of a hundred head teachers from other schools for endowed children, held at Bloor's in cb05.
The woman who looks after pupils' health and bedrooms at a boarding school. At Bloor's, Matron is Charlie's great-aunt Lucretia.
A big, formal party with dancing. In cb05 it follows the Hundred Heads' dinner.

paragraphs.context: some of the portraits had been decorated with gold ribbon.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The school is ready for visitors.
paragraphs.simple: White lights hang along the dark hallway. Some of the portraits have gold ribbon, perhaps only the relatives of the important visitors.

paragraphs.context: a sea of people moved slowly around the hall.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The hall is full of guests.
paragraphs.simple: The hall is lit by a thousand lanterns. The visitors wear many kinds of clothes: tuxedos, turbans, capes, robes, saris and kimonos.

paragraphs.context: They waited another five minutes and then jumped into their slippers,
paragraphs.simple: The boys creep down the back stairs toward the underground dining hall. They keep to the shadows, but a waitress comes out of the green kitchen with a cart.

paragraphs.context: But no way was he going into the green kitchen where the porter's wife, Mrs. Weedon, held sway.
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. Weedon, the porter's wife, rules the green kitchen. She is mean and a bad cook, and she might send the boys back to bed.

background.note: Bertha Weedon, the porter's wife. She is short-tempered and cooks for the Bloor family in the green kitchen.
The gardener and porter at Bloor's Academy. He works for the Bloors and is not friendly to the children.

paragraphs.context: Crouched in the dark, Charlie and Billy listened to the chomping,
paragraphs.mainIdea: The boys hide near the dinner guests.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie and Billy hide in the dark and hear the guests eating above them. Charlie moves, and Billy puts his hand on a foot in a silver shoe.

paragraphs.context: He put a finger to his lips.
paragraphs.simple: A man in a turban looks straight at Charlie. Charlie does not know what to do, so he asks the man to keep quiet.

paragraphs.context: "First, I must give you a brief history of someone whom even I had never heard of, until last week.
paragraphs.simple: Dr. Bloor is excited. He tells the visitors about someone from long ago whom he only heard of last week: Count Harken.

background.note: An evil enchanter from long ago who married Lilith, the Red King's eldest daughter. He hates the Red King's family.

paragraphs.context: "Fourteen years ago I was the happiest girl in the world.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs. Tilpin tells her sad story.
paragraphs.simple: She says she loved a man, but he married another woman. Later she married Matthew Tilpin, and they had a son, Joshua.

paragraphs.context: Charlie grinned encouragingly and scrambled under the red cloth
paragraphs.simple: Charlie climbs onto the bottom shelf of a cart, under a red cloth. The cloth does not cover him completely, so he stays very still.

paragraphs.context: Billy didn't appear. Charlie waited and waited.
paragraphs.simple: Billy does not come. The guests are leaving, and Charlie worries that the Bloors have caught Billy.

paragraphs.context: I always carry my candles with me,
paragraphs.simple: Billy got the key through the keyhole on a piece of paper. He was scared in the dark, so he lit one of the candles from his guardian, Mr. Crowquill.

background.note: Christopher Crowquill, a small, shy man who knows about Billy Raven's family and wants to help him.

paragraphs.context: "I know, Charlie. I heard. I can't talk about it now.
paragraphs.simple: There is no time to talk. All the head teachers will soon arrive for meetings all over the school.

paragraphs.context: Standing very still, beneath one of the trees, Charlie saw a white horse.
paragraphs.simple: It is cold and dark, and Charlie is afraid that Asa, in his beast shape, will jump out. But under a tree stands a white horse.

background.note: Manfred's friend, a drama student with red hair and yellow eyes. He is a were-beast who changes shape at dusk.

paragraphs.context: Charlie found it difficult to be patient.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie keeps asking his uncle questions. Uncle Paton only knows that Amy's invitation came from Kingdom's, the store that sent the bad prawns.

background.note: A big, expensive store in the city.

paragraphs.context: He felt that he was losing a battle.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie feels he is losing his mother.
paragraphs.simple: A man is taking Charlie's mother away with beautiful words. Charlie does not know how to fight him, so he leaves her room.

paragraphs.context: Charlie shivered. He had never seen his mother without her ring.
paragraphs.simple: Amy wears a wide silver bracelet, but her diamond ring is gone. Charlie has never seen her without it, and this frightens him.

paragraphs.context: The gold limousine glided away, as silently as a serpent.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Amy drives away in a gold car.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie runs to the door, but his mother is already in a long gold limousine. The driver gives Charlie a nasty look and drives away.

paragraphs.context: The woman was Charlie's mother, Mrs. Bone.
paragraphs.simple: Billy watches a couple come into the hall. The woman is Charlie's mother in a beautiful blue dress. Billy has never seen her like this.

paragraphs.context: Charlie's mother was holding the arm of a man in a green velvet suit.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Billy sees the man with Amy.
paragraphs.simple: Amy is with a man in a green velvet suit. He has thick brown hair touched with gold, and a nose like a hawk.

paragraphs.context: he turned out the light and put all five of his guardian's candles on the windowsill.
paragraphs.simple: Billy has a headache and needs comfort. He puts his guardian's five candles on the windowsill, and they light with a clear, steady light.

paragraphs.context: When Charlie went in he was met by Norton, the bouncer,
paragraphs.simple: Norton, the café bouncer, meets Charlie at the door. He wears a pink T-shirt with sparkling elephants on it.

background.note: The large bouncer who guards the door of the Pets' Café. Only people with pets may enter.

paragraphs.context: Tancred stamped his foot and a wild wind blew through the room.
paragraphs.simple: Tancred is angry, and his mood makes a strong wind in the café. Plates, cups and food fly everywhere.

background.note: An endowed art student with crackling blond hair. He is a storm-bringer: his moods make wind, rain and thunder.

paragraphs.context: "She's my brother's daughter, twins we are,
paragraphs.simple: The little girl is Una, the daughter of Mr. Onimous's twin brother. Mr. and Mrs. Onimous have no children, so Una is like their own daughter.

background.note: The children at Bloor's with magic powers from the Red King. Here 'endowed' means 'born with a magic gift'.
Mr. Onimous's small niece, about five years old. Her endowment is kept secret.

paragraphs.context: Homer settled the argument over who should have the last marshmallow by spearing it with his beak.
paragraphs.simple: Homer the owl takes the last marshmallow with his beak. As the friends leave the café, Charlie walks straight into Benjamin and Runner Bean.

paragraphs.context: "Much has been said of a certain mirror."
paragraphs.mainIdea: Uncle Paton talks about the mirror.
paragraphs.simple: Uncle Paton tells the children about the Mirror of Amoret. It was made for the Red King's youngest child.

background.note: The Red King's youngest child, a daughter born just before the queen died.
The Red King's wife. When she died, five of their children turned wicked.
The Red King's good second son, who sailed away to an island in the northwest.
An ancient magic mirror that once belonged to Amoret, the Red King's youngest child.

paragraphs.context: "Paton, it has just occurred to me that if the count has the mirror, he can travel again."
paragraphs.simple: Miss Ingledew suddenly understands something. If the count has the mirror, he can travel again.

background.note: Julia Ingledew, the kind owner of a bookshop near the cathedral. Uncle Paton likes her very much.

paragraphs.context: "It's getting so dark," said Mrs. Vertigo.
paragraphs.simple: Olivia's mother says it is strangely dark outside. She says sorry for interrupting the children's meeting.

background.note: Olivia's mother, a lively actress who loves bright, fancy clothes.

paragraphs.context: A man dressed for climbing smiled out at him.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie looks at an old photo.
paragraphs.simple: The photo shows Bartholomew Bloor dressed for climbing. Another man stands in the corner with his back to the camera.

paragraphs.context: Before he closed his eyes he saw the white moth sitting on the photo;
paragraphs.mainIdea: The moth sits on the photo.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie puts the photo by his bed. The face of one man in it cannot be seen. The white moth sits on it, and her wings shine softly, as if to keep him alive.

paragraphs.context: Flinging on her bathrobe, Julia ran down into the shop.
paragraphs.simple: Julia runs down into her shop at night. In the light of the streetlamp she sees two dark shapes standing outside her window, and she freezes with fear.

paragraphs.context: He was kneeling over his victim with his hands around the man's throat.
paragraphs.simple: A man in a long hooded cloak kneels over another man and squeezes his throat. In the dark, only the victim's silver hair can be seen.

paragraphs.context: There was a muffled growl of fury as the man loosened his grip and fell sideways.
paragraphs.simple: The man in the cloak lets go and rolls over the stones, wrapping himself in his cloak. Only his shining eyes can be seen.

paragraphs.context: The four survivors retreated into the shop.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The bookshop door survives the fire.
paragraphs.simple: The four people go back into the shop. Julia is glad that the thick oak door is still strong after the fire.

paragraphs.context: "Yes," he said slowly. "I could take them to Skarpo."
paragraphs.simple: Charlie thinks for a moment. He says he could take them to Skarpo.

background.note: A powerful sorcerer from long ago, seen in an old painting. Charlie travels into the picture and meets him.

paragraphs.context: The title, The Sorcerer, had been scrawled in black paint at the bottom.
paragraphs.mainIdea: An old painting of a sorcerer.
paragraphs.simple: The small painting is very old and dark. It shows a sorcerer in a black robe in a small room, with magic objects on the table behind him.

paragraphs.context: Pine needles, tinsel, broken plastic, and bits of food littered the hall floor.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The school is a mess after the visitors.
paragraphs.simple: After the hundred head teachers leave, the hall is full of rubbish. Clothes are missing from the coatrooms, and no one listens to complaints.

paragraphs.context: At last he was standing twelve feet above the crowd.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie has his back against the ancient wall. He finds places for his hands and feet and climbs high above the crowd.

paragraphs.context: Charlie saw a black cloud falling through the trees.
paragraphs.simple: The children look up and run away screaming. A black cloud of stinging insects comes through the trees, and Joshua shouts that Charlie will be stung to death.

paragraphs.context: some of the people walking down Filbert Street really strange?
paragraphs.simple: Charlie notices odd people on his street. They look into windows, touch gates, check door numbers and write notes in little black books.

paragraphs.context: They will not toe the line!
paragraphs.mainIdea: Someone will not obey the Bloors.
paragraphs.simple: The speaker hoped "he" would join them, but he is too much like his father. Neither of them wants to help with Ezekiel's plan to control things. To "toe the line" means to obey the rules.

paragraphs.context: It was embarrassing to think he couldn't take care of himself.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie feels a little embarrassed that he needs protection. But he is glad he will not be alone every time he goes out.

paragraphs.context: remembering that this was the moment he'd been waiting for, he ran into the hall and phoned Olivia.
paragraphs.simple: His mother leaves in the gold limousine without a word. Charlie is sad, but then he remembers his plan and phones Olivia.

paragraphs.context: "No time for gawking, Liv," she whispered to herself
paragraphs.simple: Olivia looks around the strange apartment: white fur on the floor, a pony-skin sofa, ivory tables and stuffed birds. She tells herself not to stare.

paragraphs.context: Empty, empty, empty. Olivia's heart sank.
paragraphs.simple: All the drawers are empty. The last one only opens a little, but at the very back Olivia feels something smooth and flat.

paragraphs.context: The smoke illusion had worked.
paragraphs.simple: Olivia slips quietly out of the apartment. Her illusion of smoke worked: the frightened guard is stamping on the carpet, trying to put out a fire.

paragraphs.context: "I'd like to be alone with it, for a while."
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie wants to be alone with the mirror.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie took the mirror to keep it away from the count. Now he wants to be alone with it. Mist covers the glass.

paragraphs.context: The mist on the glassy surface began to clear.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The moth helps clear the mirror.
paragraphs.simple: The white moth comes out of Charlie's sleeve and sits on the gold frame of the mirror. She beats her wings, and the mist starts to clear.

paragraphs.context: He remembered a bright kitchen;
paragraphs.simple: Charlie remembers a time before he lived on Filbert Street. He was very small, and his mother was humming to music from another room.

paragraphs.context: "Are you still asleep? You must remember me.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie begs his father to remember him and to say something. He shakes his father's shoulder.

paragraphs.context: he couldn't hide his fear, and his voice shook with emotion.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie tells every detail of the events as calmly as he can. But when he comes to the most important part, his voice shakes.

paragraphs.context: he almost forgot to look miserable.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie is happy to see Benjamin.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie feels hopeful and forgets to look sad. When Benjamin and Runner Bean run up to him, he shouts with joy.

paragraphs.context: Runner Bean grabbed his sleeve in his mouth and hauled him back again.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Runner Bean saves Charlie on the bridge.
paragraphs.simple: Crossing the bridge again is dangerous. Benjamin slips twice, and Charlie loses his footing, but Runner Bean pulls him back by his sleeve.

paragraphs.context: They went straight to the kitchen where they immediately lit several candles.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie and his uncle come home.
paragraphs.simple: A light is on in the living room, so they think Grandma Bone is watching TV. They avoid her and light candles in the kitchen.

paragraphs.context: She had decided to take the form of a barn owl,
paragraphs.simple: Emma hides in a dark corner by the library. She thinks of a barn owl, and her fingers slowly change into feathers.

paragraphs.context: But the blow she expected never came.
paragraphs.simple: Emma waits to be hit, but she hears a growl. A four-footed animal lands behind her and snarls.

paragraphs.context: Emma found herself gazing at a tree of astonishing beauty.
paragraphs.simple: A queen shows Emma a tree in the middle of a glade. At first it is dark, but then it fills with color, and its red and gold leaves seem to burn.

paragraphs.context: He wondered if the cracked mirror would work after all.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie watches his mother get into the car. He fears there is no time left to stop the count from taking her away.

paragraphs.context: while his wife squeezed in beside Mrs. Sage.
paragraphs.simple: The room is very full. People squeeze in wherever they can, and Tancred and Lysander share one chair.

background.note: A tall, kind African boy in the art department. He is endowed: he can call up the spirits of his ancestors.
Jessamine Sage, Lysander's mother. She understands his gift and knows when his ancestors are angry.

paragraphs.context: it was as though the tunnel were filled with moonlight.
paragraphs.simple: The five candles fill the tunnel with soft light. They also make the children feel better, and the long walk seems short.

paragraphs.context: They began their third circle.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The children walk around the tree.
paragraphs.simple: The children walk in a circle for the third time. Charlie looks away from the tears, which seem as if they will never stop.

paragraphs.context: At the top of the Music Tower, Mr. Pilgrim watched leaves dance like fireflies outside his window.
paragraphs.simple: Names move in the back of his mind. He feels as if he is swimming up through dark water. He sees a face, and then it is gone.

background.note: The tall, silent piano teacher at Bloor's Academy. He seems to live in his own world.

paragraphs.context: It had started to snow again.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Amy and Charlie go out at night.
paragraphs.simple: Late at night, Grandma Bone wakes up and finds Amy and Charlie putting on their boots and coats. Snow is falling again.

paragraphs.context: Look to the forest, if ye seek the Kinge
paragraphs.mainIdea: An old spell says to look in the forest for the king. He is hidden there.
paragraphs.simple: If you want to find the king, look in the forest. He is hidden there. The words are old.

paragraphs.context: Head teachers from a hundred other academies come here
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Hundred Heads are not a hundred heads. They are the head teachers of a hundred schools.
paragraphs.simple: Billy says the man was glad to explain. Every ten years the schools meet again. The head teachers from a hundred other academies come to talk about their pupils. That is why the dinner is called the Hundred Heads.

paragraphs.context: A piano teacher called Mr. Pilgrim
paragraphs.mainIdea: Someone was kept at the school under another name: Mr. Pilgrim, a piano teacher.
paragraphs.simple: He asks if it was a piano teacher called Mr. Pilgrim. He asks whose wicked idea it was to keep that person so near, almost under their noses.

sentences.context: Through his father, he is descended from the Red King and through his mother, from Mathonwy a Welsh magician and friend of the Red King.
sentences.simple: His father's family goes back to the Red King, and his mother's family goes back to Mathonwy.
sentences.main: He comes from the Red King and from Mathonwy.

parts.text: Through his father,
parts.meaning: On his father's side,

parts.text: he is descended from the Red King
parts.meaning: his family goes back to the Red King

parts.text: and through his mother, from Mathonwy
parts.meaning: and on his mother's side, it goes back to Mathonwy,

parts.text: a Welsh magician and friend of the Red King.
parts.meaning: a magician from Wales who was the Red King's friend.

sentences.grammar: In the second part the words "he is descended" are left out because they are the same as before.

sentences.context: The king was tall, his black hair showed not a trace of gray and his dark skin was unlined, but the sorrow in his eyes was centuries old.
sentences.simple: The king looked young, but his eyes showed a very old sadness.
sentences.main: The king was tall, but his sorrow was very old.

parts.text: The king was tall,
parts.meaning: The king was tall.

parts.text: his black hair showed not a trace of gray
parts.meaning: His hair had no gray at all

parts.text: and his dark skin was unlined,
parts.meaning: and his skin had no lines.

parts.text: but the sorrow in his eyes was centuries old.
parts.meaning: But his eyes looked sad, as if for hundreds of years.

sentences.context: The king walked around the fire with long, measured strides and the leopards followed him, around and around and around.
sentences.simple: The king walked slowly around the fire, and the leopards walked behind him again and again.
sentences.main: The king walked around the fire and the leopards followed him.

parts.meaning: The king walked in a circle around the fire

parts.text: with long, measured strides
parts.meaning: with long, slow, careful steps

parts.text: and the leopards followed him,
parts.meaning: and the leopards walked behind him,

parts.text: around and around and around.
parts.meaning: many times.

sentences.grammar: Repeating "around and around and around" makes us feel the long, slow circling.

sentences.context: The occasional flash of silver was the only hint that, moments ago, the hallway had been bristling with weapons.
sentences.simple: Only a few flashes of silver showed that the hall had just been full of weapons.
sentences.main: Only flashes of silver were left.

parts.text: The occasional flash of silver
parts.meaning: A bright silver light now and then

parts.text: was the only hint
parts.meaning: was the only sign

parts.text: that, moments ago, the hallway had been bristling with weapons.
parts.meaning: that, a short time before, the hall had been full of weapons.

sentences.grammar: "Bristling with" means "full of many sharp things". Past perfect "had been" shows the earlier time.

sentences.context: The enchanter thought he had won; Miss Chrystal had revealed herself as a witch, so now she would hide herself away before deciding on her next move.
sentences.simple: The enchanter believed he had won. Miss Chrystal had shown she was a witch, so she would hide for now.
sentences.main: The enchanter thought he had won.

parts.text: The enchanter thought he had won;
parts.meaning: The enchanter believed he was the winner;

parts.text: Miss Chrystal had revealed herself as a witch,
parts.meaning: Miss Chrystal had shown everyone she was a witch,

parts.text: so now she would hide herself away
parts.meaning: so now she would go and hide

parts.text: before deciding on her next move.
parts.meaning: before choosing what to do next.

sentences.grammar: The semicolon (;) joins two closely connected sentences.

sentences.context: They walked in single file, Benjamin stepping carefully into Charlie's footprints, both clinging tightly to the rusty rail.
sentences.simple: They walked one behind the other, holding the old rail tightly.
sentences.main: They walked in single file.

parts.text: They walked in single file,
parts.meaning: They walked one behind the other,

parts.text: Benjamin stepping carefully into Charlie's footprints,
parts.meaning: with Benjamin putting his feet where Charlie's feet had been,

parts.text: both clinging tightly to the rusty rail.
parts.meaning: and both holding hard to the old rail.

sentences.grammar: The -ing phrases with their own subjects ("Benjamin stepping", "both clinging") add details.

sentences.context: They would flow on forever, Charlie thought, until the ring of children stood knee-deep in a crimson pond.
sentences.simple: Charlie thought the red tears would never stop, and the children would stand in a red pool.
sentences.main: Charlie feared the tears would never stop.

parts.text: They would flow on forever,
parts.meaning: The tears would never stop running,

parts.text: Charlie thought,
parts.meaning: Charlie thought,

parts.text: until the ring of children stood knee-deep in a crimson pond.
parts.meaning: until the circle of children stood in a deep red pool up to their knees.

sentences.grammar: "Charlie thought" is put in the middle of the thought, a common style in stories.

sentences.context: But a cloud of bright leaves blew into the room and swept him through the window, a ball of green tumbleweed, licked by scarlet flames.
sentences.simple: Bright leaves blew into the room and carried him out of the window like a ball of burning plants.
sentences.main: Leaves swept him through the window.

parts.text: But a cloud of bright leaves blew into the room
parts.meaning: But many bright leaves flew into the room

parts.text: and swept him through the window,
parts.meaning: and carried him out of the window,

parts.text: a ball of green tumbleweed, licked by scarlet flames.
parts.meaning: like a ball of green dry plants with red fire around it.

sentences.grammar: The last phrase describes what he looked like (apposition). "Licked by flames" means flames touched it.
